item.title: Friday's Rockets-Nuggets game won't be on regular TV carrier. Here's how to watch it.
item.description: Friday's Rockets-Nuggets game is a streaming exclusive that will only air on Prime Video and Houston's usual TV carrier. (Ashley Landis/Associated Press) For the second time in the season's first month, a Houston Rockets game will require a streaming subscription to watch. Friday's 9 p.m. game against the Nuggets in Denver, which is part of NBA Cup group play, will stream exclusively on Prime Video. It will not be available on Space City Home Network, which airs the majority of Rockets games. The game is the second of four Houston games this season that will be exclusive to Prime, which is Amazon's streaming service. Michael Grady (play-by-play), Brent Barry (analyst) and Allie Clifton (sideline reporter) will call the game. In addition, two former Rockets players - John Wall (2020-22) and Kyle Lowry (2009-12) - will be part of the studio crew, joining host Taylor Rooks and fellow analyst Candace Parker. The game can be viewed on the Prime Video app or at Amazon.com . For those who already have an Amazon Prime subscription to get free or expedited shipping from the e-commerce website, that includes access to Prime Video's sports and entertainment offerings. For those without an Amazon Prime account, a 30-day free trial is available for new and qualified returning subscribers. The NBA is in the second season of an 11-year media rights deal that saw Prime Video and NBC/Peacock become national carriers, which includes select games that are exclusively on streaming services. The Rockets also have one game that will stream exclusively on Peacock, Nov. 30 against the Lakers. Subscribe There’s more to Houston with the Chronicle. Subscribe today for just 25¢. item.title: Matt Damon Reveals the Surprising Secret Behind 'The Odyssey's Epic Final Battle
item.description: When Odysseus ( Matt Damon ) finally returns home in Homer's Odyssey , he discovers that getting back to Ithaca was only half the battle. His palace has been overrun by suitors hoping to marry his wife, Penelope (Anne Hathaway), and claim his kingdom. Naturally, Odysseus isn't particularly thrilled about any of this. What follows is one of the epic poem's most memorable confrontations, as the Greek hero takes matters into his own hands.

item.title: ‘It felt like a calling': How 49ers' Christian McCaffrey is fighting for veterans
item.description: Christian McCaffrey (23) high fives George Kittle (85) after scoring in the first half as the San Francisco 49ers played the Las Vegas Raiders at Levi's Stadium in Santa Clara, Calif.,, on Sunday, Nov. 8, 2026. (Carlos Avila Gonzalez/S.F. Chronicle) AIR FORCE ACADEMY, Colo. - On Jan. 28, 2024, Bryan Flanery, a Detroit native and long-suffering Lions fan, watched his team lose 34-31 to the San Francisco 49ers in the NFC Championship Game, blowing its best chance to finally reach a Super Bowl because it blew a 17-point, second-half lead. In the aftermath, however, Flanery, 40, an Army veteran who attempted suicide in 2012, swallowing a fistful of his anti-depressant and pain pills while recovering from a cascade of traumatic injuries, felt conflicting emotions. His boyhood team's loss meant 49ers running back Christian McCaffrey had won. "Oh, man, that was a tough game," Flanery said. "But, yeah, I was happy and sad in the same moment." Like countless military veterans, along with those in active duty, Flanery supports McCaffrey because McCaffrey has committed to supporting them. Through the foundation McCaffrey established in 2021, 23 and Troops, he's worked to assist those whose service has been followed by trauma, PTSD, alcohol and drug abuse, crumbling marriages and shattered families. In February, McCaffrey, 30, received the NFL's Salute to Service Award for his commitment. His passion has its roots in his hometown of Castle Rock, Colo., which is about 30 miles from the Air Force Academy, where the 49ers are practicing this week in preparation for Sunday's game against the Vikings in Mexico City. In 2021, Flanery met McCaffrey, then playing with the Panthers, at McCaffrey's home outside Charlotte to film videos shortly after 23 and Troops launched. McCaffrey's foundation quickly partnered with REBOOT Recovery, a faith-based program that provides 12-week, trauma-healing courses. If you need help If you or someone you know is experiencing a mental health crisis, call the free 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline by dialing "988" 24 hours a day or text "HOME" to 741741 to reach a crisis counselor anytime. Flanery became a REBOOT graduate, and then a leader, after his suicide attempt. He's now led more courses than anyone in the history of a 16-year-old program that includes 64,000 graduates. Flanery has dedicated his life to serving those who are as broken as he was. In McCaffrey, he's found a celebrity athlete who hasn't merely offered his name to the cause. He's given his heart. "The man that I met (in 2021) was just as passionate about helping hurting people as I am," Flanery said. "And that's not a room that I find myself in very often." Growing up In Castle Rock, which is also close to a host of military installations, McCaffrey counted multiple military veterans among his mentors. item.content:encoded: Christian McCaffrey (23) high fives George Kittle (85) after scoring in the first half as the San Francisco 49ers played the Las Vegas Raiders at Levi's Stadium in Santa Clara, Calif.,, on Sunday, Nov. 8, 2026. (Carlos Avila Gonzalez/S.F. Chronicle) AIR FORCE ACADEMY, Colo. - On Jan. 28, 2024, Bryan Flanery, a Detroit native and long-suffering Lions fan, watched his team lose 34-31 to the San Francisco 49ers in the NFC Championship Game, blowing its best chance to finally reach a Super Bowl because it blew a 17-point, second-half lead. In the aftermath, however, Flanery, 40, an Army veteran who attempted suicide in 2012, swallowing a fistful of his anti-depressant and pain pills while recovering from a cascade of traumatic injuries, felt conflicting emotions. His boyhood team's loss meant 49ers running back Christian McCaffrey had won. "Oh, man, that was a tough game," Flanery said. "But, yeah, I was happy and sad in the same moment." Like countless military veterans, along with those in active duty, Flanery supports McCaffrey because McCaffrey has committed to supporting them. Through the foundation McCaffrey established in 2021, 23 and Troops, he's worked to assist those whose service has been followed by trauma, PTSD, alcohol and drug abuse, crumbling marriages and shattered families. In February, McCaffrey, 30, received the NFL's Salute to Service Award for his commitment. His passion has its roots in his hometown of Castle Rock, Colo., which is about 30 miles from the Air Force Academy, where the 49ers are practicing this week in preparation for Sunday's game against the Vikings in Mexico City. In 2021, Flanery met McCaffrey, then playing with the Panthers, at McCaffrey's home outside Charlotte to film videos shortly after 23 and Troops launched. McCaffrey's foundation quickly partnered with REBOOT Recovery, a faith-based program that provides 12-week, trauma-healing courses. If you need help If you or someone you know is experiencing a mental health crisis, call the free 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline by dialing "988" 24 hours a day or text "HOME" to 741741 to reach a crisis counselor anytime. Flanery became a REBOOT graduate, and then a leader, after his suicide attempt. He's now led more courses than anyone in the history of a 16-year-old program that includes 64,000 graduates. Flanery has dedicated his life to serving those who are as broken as he was. In McCaffrey, he's found a celebrity athlete who hasn't merely offered his name to the cause. He's given his heart. "The man that I met (in 2021) was just as passionate about helping hurting people as I am," Flanery said. "And that's not a room that I find myself in very often." Growing up In Castle Rock, which is also close to a host of military installations, McCaffrey counted multiple military veterans among his mentors. Their stories of commitment, discipline and sacrifice helped shape a future All-Pro known for his maniacal work ethic. After he was drafted by the Panthers in 2017, McCaffrey joined a veteran-laden team whose best players, Cam Newton, Luke Kuechly and Greg Olson among them, were active in the community partly because it was stressed by head coach Ron Rivera, who won the Salute to Service Award in 2022. McCaffrey had a sense he wanted to support the military, but he lacked a vision until he came across a sobering statistic: 22 veterans a day commit suicide. McCaffrey's uniform number with the Panthers was 22. "It felt like a calling," McCaffrey said. "It was, ‘Hey, this is unbelievable. And we have to do something about this.'" To get something done, McCaffrey's foundation has taken a holistic approach to healing. It's why 23 and Troops has also formed partnerships with Resilience Code, which provides free medical care, and the Taya and Chris Kyle Foundation, which provides marriage counseling for veterans. Before an interview for this story, a member of the 49ers public relations staff said McCaffrey had a 10-minute window to talk. But McCaffrey, a sometimes-reluctant interview subject, waved his hand when a reporter asked about the looming cutoff in mid-conversation. The gesture made it clear: McCaffrey thought the topic was too important. The interview didn't end until every question had been asked. McCaffrey, who was a communications major at Stanford, wanted to discuss many of the issues on which he's educated himself, often through meetings with those who have served. McCaffrey became particularly moved about the quality of medical care provided to veterans, which, in his view, pales to what NFL players receive. Christian McCaffrey with General Chris Donahue, the last U.S. service member to leave Afghanistan in 2021. (23 and Troops) His foundation's flagship initiative provides medical and mental-health care for Special Operations forces veterans suffering from post-traumatic stress. The program is run in conjunction with Resilience Code, whose founder, Dr. Chad Prusmack, has worked with McCaffrey for more than a decade on his athletic performance and cognitive function. McCaffrey approached Prusmack about creating comprehensive health evaluations for veterans, providing a year of no-cost personalized care. "Here I am getting the top care on planet Earth when it comes to my brain, my body, all these different images, blood work and access to treatment," McCaffrey said. "The thought was: Why don't we try to do as best we can to individualize plans for these men and women who have gone through so much?" A beneficiary of the program is Jonathan Hulecki, 45, a former Navy SEAL Commander who retired in January 2025. Hulecki said the Veteran's Affairs Office termed him "100% disabled" when he left the service. He declined to discuss the specifics of his disabilities, but he noted that many of those with whom he served during his 21-year career are dealing with "visible wounds and invisible wounds." "In SEAL teams, we're trained to operate at the highest levels both of physical and mental performance," Hulecki said. "When you take off the uniform, that commitment to excellence shouldn't end, but for a lot of guys it does. And so the challenge is learning how to apply that same mindset to your health and your family and your purpose in a civilian life. I've been fortunate to connect with some benevolent organizations." Hulecki's health workup included blood work, physical testing and neurological assessments. He met with dieticians and spoke with counselors who helped him map out his post-military life. For McCaffrey, the goal is to drive down the number of veteran suicides and create meaningful lives in their place. Hulecki is on a promising path. He's vice president of an HVAC company, leads an AI consulting firm, is an ambassador for the Navy SEAL Foundation, serves on the finance committee at his church in Virginia Beach, Va., and is an assistant coach for his son's flag football team. "You have to be able to transition to the next phase of life so that you can become excellent at something else," Hulecki said. "Christian's foundation just provides us with that platform to launch, which is amazing." McCaffrey is close friends with 49ers tight end George Kittle , who won the Salute to Service Award in 2024. Asked about McCaffrey's foundation, Kittle didn't discuss any of 23 and Troops' initiatives. Instead, he recalled a recent meeting with military families after a Saturday walkthrough practice at the 49ers' facility. McCaffrey often radiates intensity. Kittle, who gives off life-of-the-party vibes, said McCaffrey's off-the-field passion can inspire a personality transformation. "When you have a friend who is as particular as Christian is, like how he is with his routine and how he treats his body," Kittle said. "And then the second he gets out there with military families, he's got the biggest smile, supporting people and just trying to make everyone feel comfortable. I mean, watching him out there, you would have thought he was me." McCaf

item.title: Westlake volleyball set on dethroning defending state champion Southlake Carroll in finals
item.description: Westlake celebrates a point as they face off against Austin High School at Burger Center in Austin on Friday, Oct. 30, 2026. Westlake won 3-1. (Mikala Compton/Austin American-Statesman) It's time for state championships in Texas high school volleyball . Westlake made it to Saturday's Class 6A Division II title game after beating Katy Tompkins in a five-set match last week. The Chaps (41-9) will play defending state champion Southlake Carroll. The Dragons (27-11) beat Austin High last season in the state finals and this year took down Mansfield to reach the final game. The 2026 6A DII state title match is set for 4 p.m. Saturday at the Curtis Culwell Center in Garland. The game can be streamed on the NFHS network website . Here's what to know about this year's UIL state finals volleyball match between Westlake and Southlake Carroll (27-11): Playing with confidence Westlake head coach Miguel Saenz said he asks his players one question on a consistent basis: How do we get our confidence? "A lot of them, they'll say things like 'We play well' or, you know, 'We believe in ourselves," Saenz said Monday. "Which is in my mind, is not the right answer. The right answer with confidence is preparation." The Chaparrals have played 50 matches this season and while Saenz continues to prepare his players throughout the week with in-game scenarios in practice, they have executed on the court. Saenz says preparation helped the Chaps reach the state finals - their win against Tompkins was the first five-set match Westlake played all season. MORE: 50 Central Texas volleyball players who had breakout seasons MORE: Wimberley advances to UIL state volleyball finals for third straight year "I feel like we're just really solid at every position, and we don't really have any weaknesses," he said. It also helps too that as the Chaps prepare for the state finals, both teams are about even. Saenz ran the numbers and by looking at statistics for both teams (kills, assists, blocks, etc.) he called it a "wash" because even though the Dragons are statistically better at getting kills and digging up balls, the Chaps get more aces and are the better blocking team. "When you're playing against your equal, which it was the same way against Tompkins ... it really is all the other things like who's going to perform under pressure? Who is going to bounce back from mistakes?" he said. Westlake's depth is making great strides Westlake made it through to the state title game, of course, on big performances from its usual suspects. Outside hitters Geralynn Byers-Veal and Caroline Ehrlich each had 11 kills in the semifinal match and Clayton Kelly led the team with 28. Middle blocker Taylor Chorazy leads the team in blocks. But the Chaparrals have seen other players elevate their play since the postseason started. Westlake's Geralynn Byers-Veal (24) and teammates celebrate a play as Westlake and Vandegrift face off Vendegrift in Austin, Tuesday, Aug. 18, 2026. (Mikala Compton/Austin America
item.content:encoded: Westlake celebrates a point as they face off against Austin High School at Burger Center in Austin on Friday, Oct. 30, 2026. Westlake won 3-1. (Mikala Compton/Austin American-Statesman) It's time for state championships in Texas high school volleyball . Westlake made it to Saturday's Class 6A Division II title game after beating Katy Tompkins in a five-set match last week. The Chaps (41-9) will play defending state champion Southlake Carroll. The Dragons (27-11) beat Austin High last season in the state finals and this year took down Mansfield to reach the final game. The 2026 6A DII state title match is set for 4 p.m. Saturday at the Curtis Culwell Center in Garland. The game can be streamed on the NFHS network website . Here's what to know about this year's UIL state finals volleyball match between Westlake and Southlake Carroll (27-11): Playing with confidence Westlake head coach Miguel Saenz said he asks his players one question on a consistent basis: How do we get our confidence? "A lot of them, they'll say things like 'We play well' or, you know, 'We believe in ourselves," Saenz said Monday. "Which is in my mind, is not the right answer. The right answer with confidence is preparation." The Chaparrals have played 50 matches this season and while Saenz continues to prepare his players throughout the week with in-game scenarios in practice, they have executed on the court. Saenz says preparation helped the Chaps reach the state finals - their win against Tompkins was the first five-set match Westlake played all season. MORE: 50 Central Texas volleyball players who had breakout seasons MORE: Wimberley advances to UIL state volleyball finals for third straight year "I feel like we're just really solid at every position, and we don't really have any weaknesses," he said. It also helps too that as the Chaps prepare for the state finals, both teams are about even. Saenz ran the numbers and by looking at statistics for both teams (kills, assists, blocks, etc.) he called it a "wash" because even though the Dragons are statistically better at getting kills and digging up balls, the Chaps get more aces and are the better blocking team. "When you're playing against your equal, which it was the same way against Tompkins ... it really is all the other things like who's going to perform under pressure? Who is going to bounce back from mistakes?" he said. Westlake's depth is making great strides Westlake made it through to the state title game, of course, on big performances from its usual suspects. Outside hitters Geralynn Byers-Veal and Caroline Ehrlich each had 11 kills in the semifinal match and Clayton Kelly led the team with 28. Middle blocker Taylor Chorazy leads the team in blocks. But the Chaparrals have seen other players elevate their play since the postseason started. Westlake's Geralynn Byers-Veal (24) and teammates celebrate a play as Westlake and Vandegrift face off Vendegrift in Austin, Tuesday, Aug. 18, 2026. (Mikala Compton/Austin American-Statesman) "Clayton Kelly has really stepped it up with her efficiency and number of kills per set ... my second middle Annabel (McDuffee) is catching up to (Chorazy) and has played better defensively and offensively," Saenz said. He also praised second setter Ellie Ogden, who had 24 assists against Tompkins while Kyrksen Cook led the team with 30. Those signs indicate Westlake is peaking and may be able to challenge Southlake Carroll, which lost several key pieces from last year's team but returned 11 players. Southlake Carroll had to get 'over the hump' Southlake Carroll coach Leslie Jackson isn't changing much in the leadup to the state title game. She quipped it's "business as usual." "For the most part, we're just keeping things the same," Jackson said. "Then, hopefully, we can execute at a high level on Saturday." Southlake Carroll, located in the Dallas-Fort Worth area less than an hour drive from the site of Saturday's final, doesn't boast a dominant record like many potential state champions. Last year's state championship team finished 35-5. The 2026 Dragons dropped tight battles early in the season, but found their form and haven't lost a game since Sept. 11. "At the beginning of the year, we were losing a lot of our matches by like two points, three (points), four points. And so I think it was just kind of getting over the hump of getting some of these kids to believe that they could finish," Jackson said. "And I think they they got there, and now they got hot when it mattered, which is all you can really ask for as a coach." Southlake Carroll volleyball player Vanessa Glenn is pictured during her team's Class 6A Division II state semifinal win over Mansfield on Nov. 14, 2026. (Matt's Photography) Jackson added that her team plays a grueling nondistrict schedule and faces a tough slate in District 4-6A, which the Dragons won with a 13-1 mark. Those experiences, she hopes, have prepared her team for Saturday's title game with Westlake. Southlake Caroll has lost just two sets during the playoffs. "I think just trying to repeat the big situations as much as you can hopefully helps get them ready ... in the postseason," Jackson said. Dragons are daunting on defense Any team in a state title game is well-rounded. When asked, Jackson said her team shines with ball control and defense. "We got some great kids that can just defend their little tails off," she said, "and I think that they're really frustrating for a lot of attackers, and for a lot of teams because they don't go away." Jackson said her team's back row is stellar, highlighting Vanessa Glenn, Collins Alonzo and Audrey McLain. She also said setters Mariel Elizondo and Emma VanTassel excel defensively. "They all just do a great job of being super scrappy and keeping the ball off the floor," Jackson said. Sign up for the Daily Briefing from the Austin American-Statesman. item.title: Prairie View A&M at Alabama State: How to watch, date, time, TV channel
item.description: Prairie View A&M can clinch a spot in the SWAC championship game with a win. Lose and it gets complicated pending the results of three other conference games this week and next. (Elías Valverde II/The Dallas Morning News) The path has cleared up for Prairie View A&M to return to the SWAC championship game, and it's as clear as it gets. All the Panthers (6-5, 5-2 SWAC) have to do is win Saturday afternoon at Alabama State (6-4, 4-3) and they'll have a chance to defend their conference championship in two weeks. Lose, and it gets complicated. Prairie View enters the final week of the regular season with a one-game lead over Southern, the only other team that can win the West Division. If the Panthers win, their spot in the title game is clinched and the discussion ends But if Prairie View loses, then the Panthers will have to wait a week to see if Southern beats Grambling on Nov. 28 in the Bayou Classic and tiebreakers kick in. Southern, Alcorn State and Arkansas-Pine Bluff all have 4-3 records, but only Southern can win a tiebreaker of those three. Pine Bluff plays at Texas Southern and Jackson State plays at Alcorn on Saturday. Here's how the possible tiebreakers would go: Southern wins a head-to-head tiebreaker against Prairie View if it's a two-team tie. If it's a three-team tie between Prairie View, Southern and Alcorn, Southern wins because it went 2-0 against the other teams. If it's a three-team tie between Prairie View, Southern and Pine Bluff, Prairie View wins because of its divisional record, the second tiebreaker since the teams would be 1-1 against each other in the first tiebreaker among three or more teams. If it's a four-team tie between Southern, Prairie View, Alcorn State and Pine Bluff, Southern wins. Alcorn and Pine Bluff would be eliminated on the head-to-head criteria as Southern and Prairie View would be 2-1 against the other teams. Southern would then win the tiebreaker thanks to its head-to-head win over Prairie View. Prairie View A&M at Alabama State When: 2 p.m. Saturday Where: ASU Stadium; Montgomery, Ala. TV: ESPN+ with Joey Lindstrom (play-by-play) and Barrett Brooks (analyst) Radio: None 2026 Prairie View A&M football schedule Aug. 29: lost to Tarleton State, 49-30 Sept. 6: beat Texas Southern, 52-14 Sept. 12: lost to Baylor, 44-3 Sept. 19: lost to Stephen F. Austin, 31-10 Sept. 26: beat Grambling State, 21-14 Oct. 3: lost to Mississippi Valley State, 28-27 Oct. 10: lost to Southern, 28-14 Oct. 17: beat Alcorn State, 41-38 Oct. 24: beat East Texas A&M, 30-19 Nov. 7: beat Alabama A&M, 31-10 Nov. 14: beat Arkansas-Pine Bluff, 13-10 Nov. 21: at Alabama State, 2 p.m. Subscribe There’s more to Houston with the Chronicle. item.title: Lake Creek volleyball has believed all season. Now it's one win from a first state title
item.description: Lake Creek will face Abilene Wylie for the Class 5A Division II volleyball championshiop in Garland on Saturday. (Jason Fochtman/Staff photographer) Setting goals in August is relatively easy. Writing them down. Speaking them out loud. It's all very simple. Winning a state championship in November is vastly more difficult. But yet, at the end of a grueling four-month season, the Lake Creek volleyball team is on the precipice of achieving its primary aspiration. The Lions (43-10) play Abilene Wylie (39-4) for the UIL Class 5A Division II state championship at 11 a.m. Saturday at the Curtis Culwell Center in Garland. Lake Creek reached the state semifinals in 2022 but came up short. Now the Lions have another chance to secure the program's first title. "We set the goal from the beginning that we were going to make state and go to state and win state. It's one thing to say it, and it's a whole other thing to be here. So we've just kept that mindset from Day 1, that we're going to do this. Every practice before a big playoff game, I remind the kids, ‘Hey, this is not our last practice. We're not done yet.' I really do think that because of that mental piece, the kids truly believed that every single round that we weren't done. It really played into our mental game." Kane was hired to lead the Lake Creek program in 2024. After posting a 35-14 record and reaching the third round of the playoffs in her first season, the Lions took a little bit of a step back last year. item.content:encoded: Lake Creek will face Abilene Wylie for the Class 5A Division II volleyball championshiop in Garland on Saturday. (Jason Fochtman/Staff photographer) Setting goals in August is relatively easy. Writing them down. Speaking them out loud. It's all very simple. Winning a state championship in November is vastly more difficult. But yet, at the end of a grueling four-month season, the Lake Creek volleyball team is on the precipice of achieving its primary aspiration. The Lions (43-10) play Abilene Wylie (39-4) for the UIL Class 5A Division II state championship at 11 a.m. Saturday at the Curtis Culwell Center in Garland. Lake Creek reached the state semifinals in 2022 but came up short. Now the Lions have another chance to secure the program's first title. MATCHUPS: Lake Creek vs. Wylie and Cypress Ranch vs. Allen "The whole thing's surreal, honestly," Lake Creek coach Kayli Kane said. "We set the goal from the beginning that we were going to make state and go to state and win state. It's one thing to say it, and it's a whole other thing to be here. So we've just kept that mindset from Day 1, that we're going to do this. Every practice before a big playoff game, I remind the kids, ‘Hey, this is not our last practice. We're not done yet.' I really do think that because of that mental piece, the kids truly believed that every single round that we weren't done. It really played into our mental game." Kane was hired to lead the Lake Creek program in 2024. After posting a 35-14 record and reaching the third round of the playoffs in her first season, the Lions took a little bit of a step back last year. Lake Creek finished with a 19-24 mark and qualified for the postseason as a fourth-place team before losing in the second round to Friendswood. Coming back this season, Kane knew the Lions' combination of senior leadership and young up-and-coming talent could propel the program to a new level of success. Lake Creek now enters the state championship on a 10-match winning streak. The Lions have won 18 of their last 19 and have lost consecutive matches just once all season. SCHEDULE: State championships in Garland "I think it honestly started last season with our youth," Kane said. "I started three freshmen last year, and we took our lumps, and we knew we were growing and build and all of those things. I knew what we had coming back this season. I knew it was going to be something really, really special, and the kids did, too. The kids knew how talented we were, how gelled we were from the get-go because we returned pretty much almost all of our team." Lake Creek has certainly been battle-tested throughout the season. Their district was among the most competitive in the state for Class 5A with A&M Consolidated (36-9), crosstown rival Montgomery (38-12) and College Station (28-19) all vying for playoff positioning. The Lions finished tied for first with Consol at 12-2. Once the playoffs began, the experience began to pay dividends. Lake Creek swept Splendora, Port Neches-Groves and Pflugerville Weiss in the first three rounds. The Lions then leaned on the perseverance they gained from some of those tough district bouts and came out with a five-set victory against Leander Glenn in the regional final. Lake Creek then clinched its spot in the state championship with a semifinal sweep over New Braunfels last week. "That's super important to our success for sure," Kane said of the district. "The UIL puts those districts together, and that's a blessing in itself that some people don't understand. For us, most district nights are a war and a battle, and it could be any of the four or five of us winning that night. There's some districts where teams have been district champs the last 10 years, and they get knocked out in the first round. Because of the daunting district we have, I think it really plays into all of our success through the playoffs. All four of us were in the regional tournament." HIGHLIGHT A GREAT ATHLETE : Nominate a Houston high school performer for Athlete of The Week Several players have stepped up for Lake Creek during its playoff run, including senior outside hitter Ryan Mokry, who leads the team with 561 kills. Junior outside hitter Blaire Sexton (425 kills), sophomore setter Breck Tessier (1,344 assists), sophomore libero Louisa Ertischek (590 digs) and sophomore middle blocker Alexis Hammack (317 kills, 82 blocks) have also played key roles and excelled as a unit to propel the Lions into uncharted territory. Kane also credited the senior group - Mokry, Reagan Trero, Breann Joyce, Brooke Kelley, Kirsten Futch and Rachel Butler - for their efforts in keeping the team focused and providing guidance to the younger players on the roster. "They have really been such a huge part of our success with their selflessness, with their mindset of going into every single practice and pushing people in their position in front of them to make us better," Kane said. "We aren't as successful as we are without that group of seniors and their selflessness and how hard they work." Throughout the Lions' playoff run, Kane has leaned on her husband, Michael Kane, for support. Michael is the head volleyball coach at Dripping Springs and has nearly 1,000 career victories. He won the most recent of his six state titles in 2022 and has firsthand knowledge of what it's like to coach from the sideline of the Culwell Center. "My husband is my biggest fan, my biggest supporter," Kane said. "He wants nothing but my success and vice versa. … It's been really fun. I got to ride his coattails a couple of years where he's been to the state tournament, and I got to experience it from the outside looking in. Now this year, it's my turn, and I think he's been more nervous than me being in the bleachers, cheering for my team and wanting my success. It's been a really, really cool to be on this side of it and just having him there to support me and help walk me through some of these moments." When it comes to competing on the biggest stage, Lake Creek might not have the experience. But the Lions have the determination and aren't wavering from the goal they set for themselves all those weeks ago. Now they just have to keep their composure and go execute. "I expect to win," Kane said. "I think my kids expect to win, but they know it's not going to be easy. And that's what we need going into this match - belief that we can do this." item.title: Cal's Big Game stakes go beyond Stanford and straight to Tosh Lupoi's future
item.description: Cal head coach Tosh Lupoi prepares to leads his team onto the field before their game against Wagner on Sept. 19 in Berkeley. (Stephen Lam/S.F. Chronicle) It's Big Game week, which means it's time for the annual exercise in comparing and contrasting the Cal and Stanford football programs. Right now one team, Stanford, is exceeding expectations. The other, Cal, is decidedly not. This is not what many would have predicted last summer when Stanford was picked to finish last in the ACC preseason media poll and Cal was riding high with a well-regarded transferportal class (ranked 14th), a marquee quarterback, and a new coach who had alumni excited. Instead, it is Stanford, after a rough start, that has righted the ship and is 5-5. The Cardinal have a chance for both a winning season for the first time in a non-COVID year since 2018 and their first bowl berth since that year. Cal, in contrast, has lapsed into chaos. The Bears are 3-7 and the season has devolved into finger-pointing, speculation and bitter feelings. The donors who helped finance the team are angry and disappointed, and there are very real questions about not only the direction of the program under first-year coach Tosh Lupoi but also whether the school can even afford to part with him. Such is life in the new, high-finance world of college football. The Big Game isn't just about bragging rights. For most of the 21st century, the annual game has served as a measuring stick, a gauge as to how the respective programs are doing, how invested the universities are in their football teams and how effective their head football coach is. In the early 2000s, Cal had a stretch where it won seven of eight Big Games, back when Jeff Tedford had the program humming with players who would go on to become NFL legends. Stanford, during that same time was lost in the Buddy Teevens/Walt Harris years. That flipped in the second decade of this century when what Jim Harbaugh built at Stanford was inherited and improved upon by David Shaw, whose teams became national contenders. The Cardinal had a run of nine straight Big Game wins while, across the bay, Sonny Dykes' teams were scoring lots of points with little to show for it. Even in recent years, while neither team has had much to boast about and fans were largely uninterested, Cal's run of four straight Big Game wins were an indication that Justin Wilcox was relatively competent at his job, in what had become an era of sad ineptitude at both programs. The Bears went to five bowl games (though Wilcox was fired before the fifth), while Stanford declined, first under Shaw and then his successors, as its administration refused to acknowledge the new realities of college football. Both teams hired general managers, Ron Rivera at Cal and Andrew Luck at Stanford. Those men both hired new coaches this year: Lupoi and Tavita Pritchard. Now those coaches will meet in their first Big Game, an event that tends to define coaches. Stanford football GM Andrew Luck, right
item.content:encoded: Cal head coach Tosh Lupoi prepares to leads his team onto the field before their game against Wagner on Sept. 19 in Berkeley. (Stephen Lam/S.F. Chronicle) It's Big Game week, which means it's time for the annual exercise in comparing and contrasting the Cal and Stanford football programs. Right now one team, Stanford, is exceeding expectations. The other, Cal, is decidedly not. This is not what many would have predicted last summer when Stanford was picked to finish last in the ACC preseason media poll and Cal was riding high with a well-regarded transferportal class (ranked 14th), a marquee quarterback, and a new coach who had alumni excited. Instead, it is Stanford, after a rough start, that has righted the ship and is 5-5. The Cardinal have a chance for both a winning season for the first time in a non-COVID year since 2018 and their first bowl berth since that year. Cal, in contrast, has lapsed into chaos. The Bears are 3-7 and the season has devolved into finger-pointing, speculation and bitter feelings. The donors who helped finance the team are angry and disappointed, and there are very real questions about not only the direction of the program under first-year coach Tosh Lupoi but also whether the school can even afford to part with him. Such is life in the new, high-finance world of college football. The Big Game isn't just about bragging rights. For most of the 21st century, the annual game has served as a measuring stick, a gauge as to how the respective programs are doing, how invested the universities are in their football teams and how effective their head football coach is. In the early 2000s, Cal had a stretch where it won seven of eight Big Games, back when Jeff Tedford had the program humming with players who would go on to become NFL legends. Stanford, during that same time was lost in the Buddy Teevens/Walt Harris years. That flipped in the second decade of this century when what Jim Harbaugh built at Stanford was inherited and improved upon by David Shaw, whose teams became national contenders. The Cardinal had a run of nine straight Big Game wins while, across the bay, Sonny Dykes' teams were scoring lots of points with little to show for it. Even in recent years, while neither team has had much to boast about and fans were largely uninterested, Cal's run of four straight Big Game wins were an indication that Justin Wilcox was relatively competent at his job, in what had become an era of sad ineptitude at both programs. The Bears went to five bowl games (though Wilcox was fired before the fifth), while Stanford declined, first under Shaw and then his successors, as its administration refused to acknowledge the new realities of college football. Both teams hired general managers, Ron Rivera at Cal and Andrew Luck at Stanford. Those men both hired new coaches this year: Lupoi and Tavita Pritchard. Now those coaches will meet in their first Big Game, an event that tends to define coaches. Stanford football GM Andrew Luck, right, hired head coach Tavita Pritchard, his former roommate while playing with the Cardinal. (Niki Williams/For the S.F. Chronicle) Big Game losses are often the final straw for coaches. Wilcox was fired the day after Cal was drubbed by Stanford, 31-10, last November. But one year later, Wilcox's tenure doesn't look so terrible. Would Lupoi, already under fire, suffer the same fate if Cal loses to Stanford on Saturday at Memorial Stadium? Maybe not. The university is still paying out Wilcox's salary, through next year, and would owe Lupoi more than $14 million over the next four years if they let him go. But there's a lot of smoke around Lupoi. Rivera's startling comments on his weekly appearance on KNBR earlier this month only turned up the heat. "He has bumped his head a lot," said Rivera, who is Lupoi's boss. "I mean, we've talked a lot, tried to give him a lot of advice, point him in the right direction. Some of it he's been very receptive, and other portions he hasn't." Rivera, who has taken to donning a headset on the sidelines, emphasized that the final games of the season were critical. "The trajectory has to be going north," he said. "We've got to put ourselves in position to show this team is headed in the right direction. You want to show a trend you can build off of and recruit off of." The trajectory has not headed north. Instead, the Bears were embarrassed 36-7 at Virginia, the team's fourth shellacking in a row. Sophomore quarterback Jaron-Keawe Sagapolutele, whose re-commitment to Cal was a huge triumph for Lupoi, has regressed this year and will almost certainly be gone. Recruiting off this season? Selling tickets to fans? Both those things are going to be a challenge. Cal isn't just suffering in comparison to Stanford. It's hurt by what's happening 500 miles south, with UCLA's resurgence. UCLA, as close a comp for Cal as exists, is thriving under first-season head coach Bob Chesney. The Bruins are 10-0, ranked No. 4 in the country, have re-engaged their fan base and are headed for the College Football Playoff. Cal head coach Tosh Lupoi, right, shakes hands with UCLA head coach Bob Chesney after the Bruins defeated the Bears 45-24 on Sept. 5 in Berkeley. (Stephen Lam/S.F. Chronicle) Full disclosure: I am a Bruin alum who is stunned and dazzled by what's happening with UCLA football, a program I have mostly ignored for the past two decades because of its irrelevance. But I'm not the only one bringing up the comparison. Rivera himself did. "I know there's a comparison to UCLA, but the thing everybody's got to understand is that UCLA brought in a current head coach who came and brought in probably half the team he went to the playoffs … with," Rivera said on KNBR. "Tosh came in as a first-time head coach and he did bring a couple of inexperienced coordinators with him. Things didn't work out the way we needed them to work out on offense." Last summer, there was hope around Cal that the Bears could follow the Indiana blueprint: hire a new coach, get a marquee quarterback and flip the program into a national championship contender. Instead, it's the little sister school in Los Angeles that is sticking to that script. Rivera, who hired untested Lupoi, sounds like he has buyer's remorse. So do the donors who forked over millions to revitalize the Cal program. Would beating Stanford be enough to salvage the season? Subscribe There’s more to San Francisco with the Chronicle. Subscribe today for just 25¢. This article originally published at Cal's Big Game stakes go beyond Stanford and straight to Tosh Lupoi's future .

item.title: From TSU to the Dynamo, the Arana brothers are kicking their way into Houston history
item.description: After a successful youth and high school soccer career, Miguel Arana found his calling as a kicker, thriving for the Texas Southern Tigers. (Carmen Johnson/TSU Athletics) With the score tied 21-21, the ball on Southern's 29-yard line with just one second remaining, Texas Southern (TSU) head coach Cris Dishman put his faith in an 18-year-old freshman who just started playing football a few years earlier. Miguel Arana calmly jogged onto the field to get the job done, almost like he'd done it before. From 46 yards, Arana booted the ball through the uprights with nearly 10 yards to spare, giving Texas Southern a walk-off victory on homecoming night inside Reliant Stadium. After the kick, Arana celebrated with teammates as they ran toward the end zone. Once there, he hit Cristiano Ronaldo's signature "Siuuu" celebration, leaping into the air and spinning 180 degrees, landing with his feet apart while throwing his arms down and back before his teammates mobbed him for more celebration. "It's similar because there's high stakes and high pressure in the moment," Arana said to Chron. "It is a lot of pressure, but I feel like a field goal has to be harder. A penalty kick is about 12 yards away, but a field goal can be up to 50 yards. So it's different, but the pressure is definitely similar. And you've got 11 people trying to take your head off versus one goalie." Arana's game-winning kick looked like a penalty-kick winner from Ronaldo's highlight reel, like something Arana practiced in the backyard with his younger brother, Matthew. You've been working for this. This is your time,'" Miguel said. "And I felt very happy seeing that because we're both very high-level athletes who understand each other and how it feels." Few could relate more than Matthew, a 16-year-old soccer phenom who became the youngest player in Houston Dynamo history to earn first-team minutes at age 15 vs. LAFC in February. The brotherly duo from Houston keep finding ways to outdo each other, each in their own unique way. No one understands that more than the younger brother. "He's just him," Matthew said to Chron from the airport, traveling from Spain to Qatar to represent Mexico's youth national team at the FIFA U-17 World Cup. "Not everybody's seen it, but the hard work he's put in to get to where he's at is evident. Every day, he would go to the field and practice his field goals. He's the man." (Carmen Johnson/TSU Athletics) With the score tied 21-21, the ball on Southern's 29-yard line with just one second remaining, Texas Southern (TSU) head coach Cris Dishman put his faith in an 18-year-old freshman who just started playing football a few years earlier. Miguel Arana calmly jogged onto the field to get the job done, almost like he'd done it before. From 46 yards, Arana booted the ball through the uprights with nearly 10 yards to spare, giving Texas Southern a walk-off victory on homecoming night inside Reliant Stadium. After the kick, Arana celebrated with teammates as they ran toward the end zone. Once there, he hit Cristiano Ronaldo's signature "Siuuu" celebration, leaping into the air and spinning 180 degrees, landing with his feet apart while throwing his arms down and back before his teammates mobbed him for more celebration. "It's similar because there's high stakes and high pressure in the moment," Arana said to Chron. "It is a lot of pressure, but I feel like a field goal has to be harder. A penalty kick is about 12 yards away, but a field goal can be up to 50 yards. So it's different, but the pressure is definitely similar. And you've got 11 people trying to take your head off versus one goalie." Arana's game-winning kick looked like a penalty-kick winner from Ronaldo's highlight reel, like something Arana practiced in the backyard with his younger brother, Matthew. Texas Southern beats Southern on a WALK-OFF FIELD GOAL 🔥 Miguel Arana III called game 🐅 📺: @theswac https://t.co/kH5u0mNnhy - LIGHT ON COLLEGE SPORTS (@LightOnSports) October 24, 2026 "He texted me, saying, 'Let's go, man. You've been working for this. This is your time,'" Miguel said. "And I felt very happy seeing that because we're both very high-level athletes who understand each other and how it feels." Few could relate more than Matthew, a 16-year-old soccer phenom who became the youngest player in Houston Dynamo history to earn first-team minutes at age 15 vs. LAFC in February. The brotherly duo from Houston keep finding ways to outdo each other, each in their own unique way. No one understands that more than the younger brother. "He's just him," Matthew said to Chron from the airport, traveling from Spain to Qatar to represent Mexico's youth national team at the FIFA U-17 World Cup. "Not everybody's seen it, but the hard work he's put in to get to where he's at is evident. Every day, he would go to the field and practice his field goals. He's the man." Arana's fast rise with the Dynamo Matthew Arana is the youngest player to ever play first-team minutes for the Houston Dynamo, as the midfielder hopes to earn time with the Mexican national team in the future. (Amanda Loman/Houston Dynamo) Miguel and Matthew admit they don't know how they got so good at sports. Their parents, Bibiana and Miguel, did what they could to keep their boys in line, living in Rosharon, Texas, a rapidly growing suburb located 30 miles south of downtown Houston. "They wouldn't really play any sports, to be honest," Matthew said, laughing. "But they made a lot of sacrifices to get us to where we are now. So I'm really grateful for them, and they're obviously really proud of us and how far we've come. It motivates me to keep going, seeing them happy and remembering the background they come from." Both kids spent plenty of time playing soccer growing up, and their talent earned them a spot in the Dynamo's youth soccer development program , as they both dreamed of playing pro soccer beyond Houston's suburbs. While Miguel joined first, Matthew's arrival in 2021 proved to be a rocketship moment for the younger Arana brother. Matthew Arana is the youngest player to ever play first-team minutes for the Houston Dynamo, as the midfielder hopes to earn time with the Mexican national team in the future. (Amanda Loman/Houston Dynamo) "We signed him for a reason," said Dynamo head coach Ben Olsen . "We believe in him. He's a guy that we want to continue to nurture and become part of the first team." Matthew's youth is deceptive, as his talent and maturity are usually found in a player ten years his senior. He can operate as a playmaker on the wing and, as an attacking midfielder, has the vision to create scoring opportunities for others. At 14, Matthew made his professional debut in July 2025 against Austin FC II, and two months later he made his first professional start on Sept. 17 versus Tacoma Defiance, logging an assist. Five months later, Matthew signed a Homegrown contract with the Dynamo on Feb. 21, becoming the youngest first-team signing in Club history at 15 years and 176 days. Matthew's rapid rise has earned him more opportunities with the club. Olsen believes bigger and better could be on the way. Listo para representar sus raíces 🇲🇽 Matthew Arana will represent Mexico at the FIFA U-17 World Cup 2026 Qatar! https://t.co/KppNnvvasE - Houston Dynamo FC (@HoustonDynamo) November 5, 2026 "It's up to him and us to make sure he's developing in the right way to start to see real minutes, significant minutes for the first team," Olsen said. "Then hopefully he has success there, and he can move on to even bigger and better things from there. And that's the national team, that's Europe." Olsen shared that Matthew having an older brother, Miguel, is "a blessing," as he knows firsthand. Olsen's older brother, Jeremy, played collegiately at James Madison, where they were teammates. "Little brother syndrome is real, and getting the s--t kicked out of you growing up, always wanting to compete against your older brother, is a blessing," Olsen said. "It certainly was for me, and I'm sure [Matthew] Arana would say the same. You have an older brother who, in some ways, gives you a playbook for what to do and what not to do, and also someone to compete with if they're playing sports and look up to." From futbol to football for Miguel Arana After a successful youth and high school soccer career, Miguel Arana found his calling as a kicker, thriving for the Texas Southern Tigers. (Eddie Maisonet) Miguel would eventually transition to other youth soccer academies in Houston as a teenager before enrolling at Almeta Crawford High School and starring on the Chargers soccer team. That's when his dad would ask him a profession-altering question. "Junior year came, my dad said, 'Why don't you just try playing kicker just to see what happens?' And I was kind of iffy about it," Miguel admitted. After an encouraging conversation with Almeta Crawford head coach David Jackson, he joined the team. "Once I stepped out on those Friday Night Lights for the first time, I was like, 'Man, I love this,'" Miguel said. "Especially seeing how natural it was to me." Arana would end up serving as the field goal kicker for one of the best teams in the state, as Almeta Crawford finished 12-2 before bowing out in the Class 4A Division I state semifinals against Kilgore. Miguel earned a national ranking, with colleges beginning to show interest. "I really got a future for this," Miguel said. "I want to chase this." After a successful youth and high school soccer career, Miguel Arana found his calling as a kicker, thriving for the Texas Southern Tigers. (Carmen Johnson/TSU Athletics) However, his late start meant only a few schools could offer him. Texas Southern, Houston Christian and Prairie View A&M extended offers to Miguel, with the Panthers initially earning his commitment. "I ended up switching. I just thought it was best here, being close to home," Miguel said. "I didn't have to worry about paying for school." Dishman also knows that if he needs another kicker, he's got an inside connection with the family. "If his little brother is willing to come and walk on and be over there, I'm willing to have him," Dishman said with a smile. "Now I'll have two brothers."

item.title: I got to tour SpaceX's Starfactory facility in Starbase, Texas, and what I saw blew my mind
item.description: null STARBASE, Texas — I just finished covering the Starship Flight 15 mission, and SpaceXs incredible launch tower catch of the returned Ship 42 spacecraft isn't the only thing over the weekend that left me speechless. The morning of the launch (Nov. 13), SpaceX invited media on a tour of Starbase's Starfactory facility, where it manufactures and assembles both stages of its massive Starship rocket - an unprecedented behind-the-scenes look at the production and scale of SpaceX's operations, and a glimpse of things to come as Starship notches more and more milestones the more it flies. For some context, the five-story-tall Starfactory spans approximately 1 million square feet (~93,000 meters), with operations split between Starship's Super Heavy boosters and upper stage Ships, and nearly 330,000 additional square feet (30,000 square meters) of office space. SpaceX officials describe its design as one more akin to an automotive manufacturing plant than that of a typical aerospace production site, and inside, it is absolutely alive with activity. Inside Starfactory We entered through an arch-covered doorway underneath the giant "X" sign on the building's shorter face. Our media gaggle was met with curious glances as we were shown through the doors and guided onto the factory floor - few are ever able to cross that threshold outside of SpaceX employees, and our presence seemed as novel to those busy working as it was to us. Inside, we were struck with the sheer enormity of Starship's scale. Giant stainless-steel rocket parts were meticulously scattered across different subassembly stations throughout the building, with Ship nose cones, cylindrical sections and booster components all under various stages of manufacture. The sheer quantity of the hardware was staggering, and being so close to each as we walked Starfactory's throughways was an eye-opener. The exterior of SpaceX's Starfactory facility at Starbase, Texas. item.dc:creator: Josh Dinner
item.content:encoded: null STARBASE, Texas — I just finished covering the Starship Flight 15 mission, and SpaceXs incredible launch tower catch of the returned Ship 42 spacecraft isn't the only thing over the weekend that left me speechless. The morning of the launch (Nov. 13), SpaceX invited media on a tour of Starbase's Starfactory facility, where it manufactures and assembles both stages of its massive Starship rocket - an unprecedented behind-the-scenes look at the production and scale of SpaceX's operations, and a glimpse of things to come as Starship notches more and more milestones the more it flies. For some context, the five-story-tall Starfactory spans approximately 1 million square feet (~93,000 meters), with operations split between Starship's Super Heavy boosters and upper stage Ships, and nearly 330,000 additional square feet (30,000 square meters) of office space. SpaceX officials describe its design as one more akin to an automotive manufacturing plant than that of a typical aerospace production site, and inside, it is absolutely alive with activity. Inside Starfactory We entered through an arch-covered doorway underneath the giant "X" sign on the building's shorter face. Our media gaggle was met with curious glances as we were shown through the doors and guided onto the factory floor - few are ever able to cross that threshold outside of SpaceX employees, and our presence seemed as novel to those busy working as it was to us. Inside, we were struck with the sheer enormity of Starship's scale. Giant stainless-steel rocket parts were meticulously scattered across different subassembly stations throughout the building, with Ship nose cones, cylindrical sections and booster components all under various stages of manufacture. The sheer quantity of the hardware was staggering, and being so close to each as we walked Starfactory's throughways was an eye-opener. The exterior of SpaceX's Starfactory facility at Starbase, Texas. (Image credit: Josh Dinner/Future) Starbase is a unique partnership of privately-owned SpaceX property and publicly-accessible land and shoreline, which has created the unique ability for anyone with a mind to do so to drive right up to the the Starship launch pad to see the facilities up close (within a few hundred feet or so, which, as rockets go, is very, very close). Fully stacked, Starship stands more than 400 feet (120 meters) tall. Standing next to such a towering colossus on the pad is enough to drive home just how big the launch vehicle is, but standing next its segmented components inside Starfactory is even more humbling; like seeing one of Ship's upper aerodynamic flaps, which are each large enough when laid flat that you could park a pair of large SUVs on their faces with room to spare. Starbase, Texas https://t.co/NqDWwUZXv9 August 25, 2025 As our tour continued and we passed rows of nose cones under preparation for integration, numbering as high as Ship 51, one stood out from the others. In the distance, only visible for moment between the overlapping views of other Ships as we walked through the production stations, was a nose cone with a series of windows cut out of its face - undoubtedly a prototype for, or possibly even the final article that will be used as NASA's Artemis lunar lander. NASA has contracted SpaceX to develop a version of Starship capable of landing astronauts on the moon as a part of the agency's Artemis program, and this appeared to the Ship being readied for when that mission arrives. NASA is targeting Artemis IV as the program's first crewed lunar landing in 2028, and while the decision solidifying Starship as the lander tasked with that mission isn't finalized (Blue Origin is also vying for that spot with its Blue Moon lander), SpaceX is clearly operating with the intention of coming out ahead. But Artemis is clearly not SpaceX's only focus, as evident by the many, many other Ships in production that did not have window holes carved out of them.SpaceX officials said the company is currently completing about one Ship upper stage every two weeks, and one Super Heavy booster every four weeks, with overlapping production allowing multiple rockets to move through the factory simultaneously. The majority of the vehicles currently being assembled will carry stacks of SpaceX's upgraded Starlink Version 3 (V3) satellites. A photo of a Starship rocket upright in a hangar at Starfactory, shared by U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth via social media . (Image credit: U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth via X) The company's Starlink network in low Earth orbit currently consists of more than 11,000 spacecraft beaming wireless internet to SpaceX customers across the globe. All of those were launched on SpaceX's workhorse Falcon 9 rocket, with the exception of a few more than 50 delivered on Starship's two most recent test flights. Both carried V3 Starlink stacks to add to the constellation, which SpaceX officials say each added the data capacity equivalent to ten Falcon 9 Starlink launches. And, as they fine tune Starship's design, SpaceX plans to increase the vehicle's launch cadence dramatically, growing the Starlink network as it does. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has stated the company hopes to launch Starship about once a week beginning in 2027, and with the number of Ships we saw lined up inside Starfactory, launch vehicle inventory doesn't seem like it will be to blame if that goal isn't realized. Building rockets like cars (and Lego bricks) SpaceX has adopted a manufacturing process modeled after the automotive industry, where efficiency and reproduction allow for the manufacture of large numbers of identical parts. Automation is a critical part of that process, but not one SpaceX is ready to entirely rely on. Much of the equipment and tools being used for Starship's production were designed by SpaceX engineers, who are constantly refining production processes to eliminate bottlenecks. And SpaceX has deliberately kept technicians on the floor as Starship's design continues to evolve, rather than automating procedures that might soon become obsolete. Our tour guide compared SpaceX's manufacturing consistency goals to that of Lego bricks, which are famously precise in their production down to the micro-millimeter accuracy of what now number more than 1 trillion bricks made since the toy company began in the 1940s. Expansion Exiting the far side of the building, we stood in the shadow of SpaceX's two towering Mega Bays, where the sections of Starship are stacked and integrated with their engines - there's one hanger for Ship, and another for Super Heavy. Each can hold about five or six assemblies, and housed two or three vehicles at the time our tour was brought by. Both Mega Bays, however, looked small against the adjacent Gigabay SpaceX is currently constructing. At approximately 700,000 square feet (65,000 square meters), Gigabay will be equipped with room to accommodate up to 24 vehicles at a time, and will facilitate a major increase in SpaceX's ability to assemble its Ship and Super Heavy rockets. Part of SpaceX's goal with Starship is to make all of what we got to see completely routine; to make rocket launches and landings as ordinary as commercial airline flights. Still, standing inside Starfactory, surrounded on all sides by huge spacecraft in various stages of assembly, it was hard to imagine a reality where giant rockets flying to and from space on a regular basis wouldn't feel like science fiction. Later that day a giant rocket launched to outer space - Super Heavy did attempt a return to pad, but was diverted for an offshore landing instead, where it exploded. But the next day, Ship 42 came plunging through the overcast cloud cover, falling belly-first toward the same tower it left just a couple dozen hours before. And then it lit its engines and was caught by the tower. That felt like science fiction too.

item.title: Draymond Green Hails Klay Thompson’s Return To 2019 Form In Miami
item.description: Credit: Isabella Frias-Imagn Images Draymond Green has watched Klay Thompson play for years, but the veteran forward sees a spark in Miami that feels rare. Green told listeners on his podcast that he has not seen Thompson play with this much spirit since 2019. The Miami Heat are now 9-6 after a rough start, and Thompson’s shooting has been a huge part of that change. Thompson struggled early in the season, shooting just 32.4 percent from the field during the team’s 0-4 start. He faced heavy pressure to be the player he was in Golden State, but Green warned fans not to expect the 2017 version of Thompson to show up. Green spoke up to protect his former teammate from unrealistic expectations that could lead to unfair criticism. Before the season began, Green urged fans to lower their sights on Thompson given his career stage. The former Dallas guard had just finished his worst shooting season, averaging 11.7 points on 39.3 percent shooting. Green felt people were setting Thompson up for failure by acting like the old version was coming to Miami. He said on his show, according to Yahoo Sports , “The reason I don’t like it is because I feel like everybody’s trying to set Klay up for failure.” He added that people should stop acting like “2017 Klay is going to Miami.” Instead of fading away, Thompson found his rhythm after those early losses. Against the Indiana Pacers, he tallied 25 points before exploding for a season-best 30 versus the Los Angeles Clippers. The game against the Los Angeles Clippers included eight three-pointers and a game-winning shot at the buzzer. Green noted that the excitement and joy Thompson is bringing to the games is beautiful to watch. The Bench Boosts Wiggins While Thompson found his stroke, Andrew Wiggins found a new role that unlocked his game. Head coach Erik Spoelstra moved Wiggins to the bench after early struggles as a starter. Wiggins had been a regular starter since joining Miami in the 2024-25 season, but the move helped him adapt to a different pace. In his last four games off the bench, Wiggins averaged 12 points, 2.5 rebounds, and 1.5 assists. He shot 53.3 percent from the field and 40 percent from three-point range during that stretch. Spoelstra praised Wiggins for his energy and effort, noting that the game rewards hard work. The coach said, according to ClutchPoints , “You know, the game usually rewards effort and energy, and it’s doing that for Wiggs right now.” Giannis Brings a Cold Stare The team’s turnaround also features a new star who has embraced the Heat culture without looking back. Giannis Antetokounmpo led Miami to a 137-130 victory over his former team, the Milwaukee Bucks, on Wednesday night. He scored 27 points and grabbed 14 rebounds in a game that felt more about winning than nostalgia. Antetokounmpo made it clear that he is not dwelling on the past or his history with Milwaukee. item.title: UFC Qatar bout to go ahead after 20-3 fighter gets fined for missing weight
item.description: Photo by Chris Unger/Zuffa LLC Tahir Abdullayev has forfeited a portion of his purse. The 20-3 welterweight is among those in Doha ahead of Saturday’s UFC Fight Night event in Qatar. Abdullayev’s clash with 24-fight Octagon veteran Jake Matthews will be one of the matchups setting the stage for the light heavyweight main event between former UFC champion Jiri Prochazka and Navajo Stirling. The Azerbaijani’s bout was briefly up in the air, however, after he failed to hit the divisional weight limit on Friday. Jake Matthews vs Tahir Abdullayev to go ahead at UFC Qatar despite weight miss It was nearly a perfect weigh-in ahead of UFC Qatar, with 23 out of the 24 fighters successfully cutting enough pounds to make their fights official. The only failure on the scale was Abdullayev, who came in at 172 pounds, one pound over the weight limit for non-title bouts in the welterweight division. He will still get the chance to impress at the ABHA Arena. The UFC confirmed soon after the weigh-ins that his fight with Matthews will go ahead, with the Azerbaijani star forfeiting 20 percent of his purse. The weight miss comes ahead of Abdullayev’s second fight in the promotion. ‘Tank’ made a successful debut this past June by stopping Jefferson Nascimento in round three. He is facing a much more experienced opponent in Matthews, a once highly-touted Australian welterweight who has failed to live up to his promise so far. Photo by Ed Mulholland/Zuffa LLC After his defeat at UFC 334 last Saturday, Jim Miller admitted regret over accepting the fight against a massively overweight Terrance McKinney. With his opponent only missing weight by one pound, Matthews may have faced an easier decision to meet Abdullayev inside the Octagon. Read more: NFL star genuinely thinks he has ‘good chance’ to become MMA fighter when football career is done UFC champion Sean Strickland goes off on ’embarrassing’ young men over playing GTA 6 Jake Paul’s next opponent admits he contemplated retirement ahead of long-awaited return

item.title: Nick Wright thinks Tom Brady has got his assessment of the Chicago Bears all wrong
item.description: Photo by Sam Hodde/Getty Images Tom Brady’s power rankings have become the barometer for how good an NFL team truly is, but his assessment of the Chicago Bears has not been widely accepted. The Bears were not in action in Week 10, as they enjoyed their bye on the back of four consecutive victories. Although the Bears did slip down from the top spot in the NFC North to third over the weekend, they still hold the same record as the Detroit Lions and Minnesota Vikings. Despite not playing, Brady kept the Bears at the top of his power rankings this week, but Fox Sports’ Nick Wright has not agreed with Brady’s verdict on Ben Johnson’s team. Despite beating the Seattle Seahawks comfortably, Wright does not see them as one of the top-tier teams. Nick Wright pushes back on Tom Brady’s Chicago Bears verdict Brady’s top five power rankings had the Bears in first, followed by the San Francisco 49ers, Buffalo Bills, Denver Broncos and Jacksonville Jaguars. Wright was quick to push back on just how highly Brady thinks of the Bears. “I think the Bears are one tier below. I think the three best teams in football are San Francisco, Kansas City, and Jacksonville. Those are the teams that, for me, check the boxes: Trust of the coach. Trust of the quarterback. Can beat you in multiple different ways? Don’t have an obvious flaw on either side of the ball,” Wright said on First Things First. Again, none of them are perfect teams, but they can beat you passing or running, they have solid defences, you trust the coach, all of it.” “I have the Bears in that next group of teams along with: Minnesota, whose question mark is their offence as a whole (we’ll see how much Kirk fixes it). Cincinnati: their question mark is, well, it’s not really a question mark. They don’t run the ball very well, but they haven’t needed to at this point. We’ll see if the weather changes and the competition gets harder. Buffalo: don’t love their secondary. “Chicago: there isn’t one thing about Chicago that I specifically don’t like. We can show you their rankings: they’re a well-rounded, solid team on both sides of the ball. It’s pretty good. Absolutely, they are; it’s them, Kansas City, and Jacksonville as the only teams that are top eight in offence and defence, points and yards, like the only teams that are top ten in all three of those categories. “I just don’t view them as consistent as those first three teams I mentioned, and because they don’t have the track record (to your point, the coach or the quarterback), I just have them one tick beneath.” Ironically, the Bears face the Jacksonville Jaguars – who Wright rates highly – in just a matter of weeks. Johnson’s team also still has to play the Lions twice, Minnesota again, and the Buffalo Bills before the end of the regular season. Whether you agree with Wright’s assessment of the Bears or not, they are going to have the opportunity to prove themselves as one of those top teams before the regular season comes to an end. item.title: 🏀 Y! Sports AM: Two-man race
item.description: Yahoo Sports AM is our daily newsletter that keeps you up to date on all things sports. Sign up here to get it every weekday morning. 🚨 HEADLINES 🏈 Belichick, Kraft named HOF finalists: Bill Belichick and Robert Kraft, the Patriots' former coach and current owner, advanced to the final round of voting for the Pro Football Hall of Fame's Class of 2027 after both were passed over for induction last year. ⚽️ Infantino's challengers: Gianni Infantino will officially face two challengers for the FIFA presidency in March's election: France's Philippe Diallo and Japan's Kohzo Tashima. Infantino's once-assured reelection bid hit turbulence this summer over his support for a 64-team World Cup and a scrapped plan to sell World Cup stakes to private investors. 🏈 Houston routs Indy: The Texans cruised to a 26-3 victory over the Colts on "Thursday Night Football" for their first home win of the season, improving to 4-6 to keep their narrow playoff hopes alive. ⚾️ Trump pardons Rose: A year after playing a role in Pete Rose's MLB reinstatement, President Trump has posthumously pardoned the all-time hits leader, who pled guilty to filing false tax returns in 1990. Rose could be inducted into the Hall of Fame as early as 2028. 🏈 NFL stars punished: Rams WR Puka Nacua was suspended three games for violating the NFL's personal conduct policy, a ban that coincides with his IR stint; Ravens CB Marlon Humphrey was sent home from the team facility and will be inactive for this week's game after saying earlier this week that Baltimore is "best at making criminals." See what else is trending on Yahoo Sports . 🏀 THE NBA MVP RACE IS A TWO-MAN SHOW Welcome to Charted Territory with Neil Paine, a new daily-ish segment from our resident stats nerd and chart-making maestro. Data never looked so good. For nearly a decade, the NBA MVP award has belonged to an exclusive club: Giannis Antetokounmpo, Nikola Jokić and Shai Gilgeous-Alexander have won eight of the past nine trophies , with Joel Embiid the lone exception. But this season, the MVP conversation has become almost entirely about two different names. Two-man race: According to a consensus of prediction market odds from Polymarket and Kalshi , Victor Wembanyama (41%) and Luka Dončić (39%) have a combined 80% chance of winning the award. Only one other player — reigning MVP SGA (6%) — even cracks 5%, with Wemby and Luka basically quadrupling the odds of the rest of the field combined. A clash of superstars: Dončić leads the NBA in scoring at an absurd 38.1 points per game, a full 7.0 clear of anyone else and on pace for the highest average since Wilt Chamberlain in 1962-63. Meanwhile, Wembanyama is averaging 28.6 points, 11.9 rebounds and a league-high 3.9 blocks while leading the league in both Win Shares and Player Efficiency Rating . 💬 MANFRED TALKS DOWN TURKEY DAY "Commissioner, any comment on why you're down on Thanksgiving?!" (Cole Burston/Getty Images) As a lockout approaches, nothing will keep MLB commissioner Rob M

(Cole Burston/Getty Images) As a lockout approaches, nothing will keep MLB commissioner Rob Manfred from the negotiating table, not even Thanksgiving. Bah humbug: The commissioner told media on Wednesday that the league will keep the lines of communication open as Dec. 1 approaches, catching Turkey Day with an undeserved stray. "A decision on a lockout is one we're going to make at the last possible moment. We're going to devote ourselves to the bargaining process. I'm not that big on Thanksgiving as a holiday. We'll make ourselves available whenever and wherever to bargain in an effort to make an agreement." No follow up: But why is Manfred down on Thanksgiving? Does he find turkey dry? Is he not a big sides guy? Prefers cake to pie? Barring a Thanksgiving miracle, a lockout appears likely, as he also noted owners are unwilling to compromise on a salary cap and floor . item.title: ‘So painful’ – Victor Wembanyama makes unexpected admission about avoiding dunks
item.description: Photo by Ronald Cortes/Getty Images San Antonio Spurs star Victor Wembanyama now actively avoids dunking the basketball. At 7’4″, San Antonio Spurs star Victor Wembanyama is one of the tallest players in the NBA right now. Evidently, when Wembanyama is near the rim, fans expect him to take advantage of his height and ruthlessly dunk the basketball. However, during the Spurs’ recent 124-112 win over the Los Angeles Clippers, Wembanyama pulled off a rather surprising move when he shot the ball from above the rim instead of dunking it. Victor Wembanyama is avoiding dunks due to a blister on his hand While the move instantly went viral on social media, many fans were left wondering why Wemby went through the trouble of shooting from above the rim instead of performing a simple dunk. The commentators called it a ‘shunk,’ but there was a real reason behind his shot choice, and it’s a painful one. “I’m not going to lie. Actually, I’ve had this blister forever, and it’s killing me. And every time I dunk, it kills me. I’ve been dragging this blister for I don’t know how long because of dunking. “So, I did not [quit dunking], but if I can avoid it, I would,” Wembanyama said. Well, that’s a sigh of relief for Wemby fans, as he has not retired from dunking, but it’s a simple makeshift adjustment until the blister on his hand heals. Either way, the blister has hardly restricted Wembanyama from stuffing the box score, as he dropped 32 points, 11 rebounds, and 3 assists against the Clippers.
